scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

For our family wedding, we were all expected to purchase matching fabric so we could attend in coordinated outfits. Would you have bought the fabric?

Here’s a balanced perspective to consider: ### **Potential Benefits:** 1. **Unity & Tradition** – If the wedding has a strong family tradition of coordinated outfits (e.g., bridesmaids, groomsmen, or even extended family), it can feel meaningful and symbolic. 2. **Photography** – Matching fabrics can create cohesive, visually striking photos, especially if everyone is wearing complementary colors or patterns. 3. **Ease of Coordination** – If you’re not great at matching outfits, this ensures everyone looks intentional and put-together. 4. **Sentimental Value** – Some families cherish the idea of "matching" as a way to honor the couple or create a shared memory. ### **Potential Drawbacks:** 1. **Cost** – Buying fabric (especially high-quality or custom-made) can be expensive, especially if multiple people are involved. Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. Would you like help brainstorming specific outfit ideas based on the wedding’s theme or your personal style? Or would you prefer tips on negotiating the expectation with your family?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex, emotionally charged situation**, and there’s no universally "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on values, priorities, and the dynamics of your family. However, I’d argue that **you’re not *inherently* in the wrong**, but you’re navigating a **highly sensitive tradition with imperfect solutions**. Here’s why: ### **Why You Might Not Be "Wrong" (or at least not *solely* wrong):** 1. **Your Family’s Tradition Was Built on *Your* Mom’s Efforts** - The 50-year tradition was *her* creation, not yours. She’s the one who made it happen for decades, and now she’s asking *you* to carry it forward. It’s not unreasonable to feel conflicted when your own family’s needs (especially your wife and daughter’s) are also valid. 2. **This Is a "Once in a Lifetime" Event** - Your wife and daughter haven’t seen their aunts/cousins in years, and the Macy’s Parade is a rare opportunity. **Family bonds matter**, and if this trip could strengthen those relationships, it’s not selfish to prioritize it. 3. **You Tried to Offer Solutions** - You proposed renting a space, swapping with your brother, or even hosting the next holiday. That shows you’re thinking about the family’s needs, not just your own. The fact that your sister rejected those solutions suggests this isn’t just about logistics—it’s about **control and tradition**. 4. **Your Sister’s Reaction Feels More About *Her* Frustration Than *Your* Guilt** - Her anger seems to stem from: - **Resentment** ("Mom wouldn’t abandon Thanksgiving"—implying *she* would have done better). - **Loss of Control** (she’s been planning her turn for a year, and now it’s disrupted). - **Guilt-Tripping** ("Mom will be sad")—which is a common emotional manipulation tactic in family dynamics. - She’s not wrong for feeling upset, but her response is **more about her expectations than your actions**. 5. **You’re Not Abandoning the Tradition—You’re Adapting It** - The tradition was always about *your mom’s* vision. Now that she can’t host, the family is figuring out how to keep it alive. **Change is inevitable**—the fact that your sister can’t renovate her house or your brother’s wife isn’t enthusiastic shows this isn’t a permanent solution. --- ### **Why You Might Feel Guilty (Even If You’re Not "Wrong")** - **Family Loyalty Pressure:** You were raised to value tradition, and breaking it (even to attend a meaningful event) can feel like betrayal. - **Your Sister’s Emotional Reaction:** Her anger might make you doubt yourself ("Am I being selfish?"). - **Your Mom’s Expectations:** She asked *you* to take over, and now you’re not fulfilling that role—even if you’re offering alternatives. - **The "Once in a Lifetime" Argument Backfires:** Some people (like your sister) might see it as an excuse rather than a valid reason. --- ### **Where the Real Conflict Lies** This isn’t just about **hosting Thanksgiving**—it’s about: - **Who gets to define family traditions?** (Your sister wants to keep the *exact* same structure; you’re open to evolution.) - **How much should we prioritize *our* family vs. *her* family?** (Your wife/daughter’s relationships with their relatives are just as valid.) - **Who gets to be the "good kid" vs. the "selfish one"?** (Your sister is framing this as a moral failing.) --- ### **What Would Be the "Right" Thing to Do?** There’s no perfect answer, but here’s how I’d break it down: #### **If You Value:** ✅ **Your wife and daughter’s happiness** + **their family bonds** → **You’re not wrong for going.** The tradition was built on your mom’s efforts, not yours. If this trip means something to your family, it’s worth it. ✅ **Keeping the Thanksgiving tradition alive** (but in a new way) → **Find a compromise:** - **Host a smaller, intimate gathering** (just immediate family) on Thanksgiving, then attend the parade on **Black Friday** (if possible). - **Record the parade** and have a post-parade dinner with your mom and siblings. - **Let your brother host Thanksgiving** (even if it’s not his turn) and swap with him for Christmas. ✅ **Avoiding conflict with your sister** → **You can’t control her reaction**, but you can: - **Acknowledge her feelings** ("I know this is important to you, and I’m sorry it’s not working out this way."). - **Offer to help her plan her Christmas** (since she’s hosting next). - **Let her vent**, but don’t let her guilt-trip you into staying. #### **If You Feel Guilty:** - **Remind yourself:** You’re not replacing your mom—you’re **adapting** the tradition to fit the new family dynamic. - **Your sister’s anger isn’t about you.** It’s about her **fear of losing control** over how the tradition is carried forward. - **Your wife and daughter’s joy matters.** If this trip brings them closer to their family, that’s a win. --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (You’re Not Wrong, But You’re in a Tough Spot)** You’re not the bad guy here—**the system is flawed**. The tradition was built on one person’s labor for decades, and now the family is struggling to keep it alive without her. **Your sister’s reaction is more about her discomfort with change than your actions.** **The "right" move depends on what you prioritize:** - If **your family’s happiness** (especially your wife and daughter’s) is more important than the exact structure of Thanksgiving, then **go to the parade**. Offer to make it up to your siblings in another way (e.g., hosting Christmas, helping with planning). - If **preserving the tradition as-is** is non-negotiable, then **host a smaller gathering** and find another way to attend the parade (even if it’s just watching it together later). **You’re not obligated to sacrifice your own family’s needs for a tradition that wasn’t *your* responsibility to uphold.** That said, **how you communicate this** (with empathy and openness to compromise) will determine how smoothly this goes. Would you like help drafting a message to your sister to explain your decision in a way that minimizes conflict?
